function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository, followed by a short “how‑to” guide for adding, committing and pushing the changes.

> **NOTE** – The repo is assumed to be cloned locally in a folder called `nodejs-welcome`.  
> If you cloned it somewhere else, just replace the paths accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile (root of the repo)

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Node 18 (Alpine for a small footprint)
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on (adjust if needed)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the official Node 18 Alpine image – small, secure, and up‑to‑date.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`) so the image stays lean.  
> * Exposes port **3000** – the common default for many Node apps; change it if your app uses a different port.

---

## 2. Kubernetes manifests

Create a folder called `k8s` at the root of the repo and add two files:

### 2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # will be built/pushed by GitHub Actions
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

### 2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80          # external port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deployment creates 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Service exposes the app internally on port 80, routing traffic to the container’s port 3000.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file called `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    # Checkout the repo
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    # Set up Docker Buildx (needed for multi‑platform builds)
    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

    # Log in to Docker Hub (or any registry you use)
    - name: Login to DockerHub
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    # Build and push the image
    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    # Optional: Deploy to a Kubernetes cluster
    # Uncomment the block below if you want automatic deployment
    #
    # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
    #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
    #   with:
    #     manifests: |
    #       k8s/deployment.yaml
    #       k8s/service.yaml
    #     kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to set in the repo settings**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username (or any registry you’re using).  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token with push rights.  
> * `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` – optional, only if you enable the deployment step.

---

## 4. Add, commit and push

Open a terminal, navigate to the repo root (`nodejs-welcome`) and run:

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the main branch
git push origin main
```

> **What happens next?**  
> * GitHub Actions will automatically trigger on the push to `main`.  
> * It will build the Docker image, push it to Docker Hub, and (if you uncommented the deployment step) apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Docker image** – After the workflow finishes, verify the image exists on Docker Hub:  
   `docker pull <your-username>/nodejs-welcome:latest`

2. **Kubernetes** – If you have a cluster configured, apply the manifests manually to test:  
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
   ```

3. **Service** – Check that the service is reachable (e.g., via `kubectl port-forward svc/nodejs-welcome-service 8080:80` and then `curl http://localhost:8080`).

That’s it! You now have a fully automated CI pipeline that builds, pushes, and (optionally) deploys your Node.js app. Happy coding!
